prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Apple Inc." (ticker AAPL), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "AAPL", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Apple Inc.
markets: Digital services (App Store, iCloud, Apple Music, Apple TV, AppleCare, Apple Pay, search licensing)
Wearables and home (Apple Watch, AirPods, HomePod, Apple TV)

mission.plain: Apple tries to make easy-to-use, beautifully designed devices and services that fit together and help people create and connect.

about.plain: Apple makes the iPhone, Mac computers, iPads, Apple Watches and AirPods. It also writes the software that runs on them, like iOS. It earns money from apps, music, TV shows, cloud storage and payments people use on those devices. Everything is designed to work together, so once people own one Apple product they often buy more.
about.customers: Ordinary people all over the world, plus schools and businesses that give Apple devices to staff.
about.everyday: The iPhone in many people's pockets and the App Store they download games from are made by Apple.

money.plain: App Store, iCloud, Apple Music, TV+, AppleCare, Apple Pay, Google search fees
Apple Watch, AirPods, HomePod, Apple TV box
A headset that mixes apps with the real world

result.summary: Apple has a wide moat built on a premium brand and an ecosystem of hardware, software and services that makes switching away painful for its more than 2 billion active devices. Its in-house Apple silicon and huge scale give it cost and performance advantages, and its Services arm turns that installed base into a growing, high-margin recurring revenue stream.

pricingPower.evidence: Apple sells about 20% of the world's smartphones but captures most of the industry's profits; it raised the iPhone 17 Pro starting price to $1,099 in 2025 yet iPhone revenue grew, and record June-quarter 2026 sales rose 16% to $109.4B at a 50.1% gross margin.

moats.evidence: Apple is consistently ranked the world's most valuable brand (Interbrand, Kantar), letting it charge premium prices across iPhone, Mac and Watch.
iMessage, FaceTime, iCloud photos, purchased apps, AirPods and Apple Watch pairing all tie users to iOS, and iPhone loyalty rates are commonly estimated above 90% in the US.
The App Store's huge base of high-spending users attracts developers who build for iOS first, and iMessage 'blue bubbles' create social pressure among US teens.
Buying for roughly 250 million iPhones a year (247.8M shipped in 2025) gives Apple first access to TSMC's newest process nodes and better component pricing than rivals.
Consumer electronics markets are large and contested by Samsung, Xiaomi and many others, so there is no natural limit on competitors.
Apple's privacy stance (App Tracking Transparency, on-device AI) is hard for ad-funded rivals like Google and Meta to copy without hurting their business model.
Tight integration of custom chips (A-series, M-series, C1 modem), software and industrial design, plus world-class supply chain management, is extremely hard to replicate.
Priority access to TSMC's leading-edge capacity and an installed base of over 2 billion active devices are unique assets, though no single exclusive resource locks rivals out.

customers.evidence: Apple tops customer-satisfaction surveys such as the ACSI for smartphones and PCs, and iPhone owners show very high repurchase rates, with the active installed base passing 2.35 billion devices in 2025.

talent.evidence: Apple is a top-ranked employer in surveys such as Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies (#1 for many years) and attracts top engineers, though it has lost some AI researchers to Meta and OpenAI.

product.evidence: Apple's M-series and A-series chips lead independent benchmarks on performance per watt, and iPhone, MacBook Air and AirPods regularly win best-in-class reviews; its weak spot is generative AI, where Siri lags Google Gemini and ChatGPT.

competitors.name: Samsung Electronics
competitors.note: Galaxy smartphones, tablets, watches and earbuds; the closest rival in premium phones

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google)
competitors.note: Android, Pixel phones, Play Store, YouTube and Gemini AI; also pays Apple for default search

competitors.name: Xiaomi
competitors.note: Smartphones, tablets and wearables, strong in China, India and emerging markets

competitors.name: Huawei
competitors.note: Premium smartphones (Mate, Pura) and HarmonyOS ecosystem in China

competitors.name: Microsoft
competitors.note: Windows PCs and Surface versus Mac and iPad; cloud and productivity services

competitors.name: Lenovo Group
competitors.note: World's largest PC maker; Motorola smartphones and tablets

competitors.name: vivo
competitors.note: Smartphones in China, India and Southeast Asia

competitors.name: Dell Technologies
competitors.note: Laptops and desktops competing with Mac in business

competitors.name: HP Inc.
competitors.note: Laptops and desktops competing with Mac

competitors.name: Amazon
competitors.note: Prime Video, Amazon Music, Kindle, Fire tablets and Alexa/Echo smart home devices

competitors.name: Meta Platforms
competitors.note: Quest headsets and Ray-Ban Meta glasses competing with Vision Pro and future Apple glasses

threats: Falling behind in generative AI: a revamped Siri was delayed and Apple relies partly on Google Gemini, while rivals build AI-first devices (e.g. OpenAI's hardware with Jony Ive)
Antitrust and regulation: the EU Digital Markets Act, US DOJ lawsuit and Epic ruling forcing App Store fee cuts and alternative payment links
Loss or reduction of Google's roughly $20B-a-year default search payments after the US search antitrust case
US-China tensions and tariffs, given heavy manufacturing in China and roughly a fifth of sales from Greater China, where Huawei has regained share
Lengthening smartphone replacement cycles in a mature market
Leadership transition from Tim Cook to John Ternus in September 2026 and departures of senior AI and design talent

ceo.name: John Ternus
ceo.background: Mechanical engineer (BS, University of Pennsylvania); joined Apple's product design team in 2001 and led hardware engineering before succeeding Tim Cook, who became executive chairman

c1.evidence: Apple leads premium smartphones (19.7% of 2025 shipments, #1 per IDC) and wearables, but these are mature markets rather than fast-growing emerging ones.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Apple for its trusted brand, ease of use, privacy and an ecosystem where iPhone, Mac, Watch and AirPods work seamlessly together, an advantage built over decades and hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Apple is one of the most recognised brands on earth, the default premium phone in the US, and tops satisfaction surveys such as ACSI, so owners widely recommend it.

c4.evidence: Apple repeatedly stresses making tools that empower people, privacy as a human right and carbon neutrality by 2030, but it does not publish a single official mission statement and is also highly profit-focused.

c6.evidence: “premium, sleek, expensive, easy to use” — the impression is mostly positive, though some see Apple as overpriced and controlling.

c7.evidence: Its markets (about 1.26 billion smartphones a year plus PCs, wearables and digital services) are huge, but core hardware is mature; growth comes from services, AI-driven upgrades and new categories.

c8.evidence: Vision Pro spatial computing, health features, in-house chips and modems, payments and possible smart glasses offer room to expand, but past bets like the Apple car project were cancelled in 2024.

m1.evidence: John Ternus only became CEO on 1 September 2026 and has not yet laid out a public long-term vision beyond continuing Apple's hardware-led product roadmap.

m2.evidence: Ternus is not a founder, but a 25-year Apple veteran who rose through hardware engineering and is seen as a long-term product steward.

m4.evidence: Ternus is described by colleagues as collaborative and low-key, but there is too little public record of his leadership as CEO to judge.

m5.evidence: Ternus inherits Apple's distinctive secretive, design-led culture created by Steve Jobs; as hardware chief he oversaw new products such as iPhone Air and M-series Macs, but he did not create the culture.

m6.evidence: A mechanical engineer by training, Ternus led hardware engineering for iPhone, iPad, Mac and AirPods before becoming CEO.

m7.evidence: There is no clear public record yet of Ternus's stewardship priorities beyond continuing Apple's commitments on privacy, accessibility and its 2030 carbon-neutral goal.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by John Ternus at Stanford, Harvard or MIT is known; predecessor Tim Cook spoke at MIT in 2017.

m8b.evidence: Ternus is a calm, low-profile engineer rather than a flamboyant public personality like Elon Musk.

m9.evidence: As hardware chief Ternus delivered the Apple silicon Mac transition and iPhone lines, but he has only a few weeks' record as CEO; under Tim Cook revenue rose from $108B (FY2011) to $416B (FY2025).

m10.evidence: Apple is known for disciplined supply-chain costs but spends lavishly on design, retail stores and its $5B Apple Park campus, so it is not known for frugality.

c10.evidence: More than 2 billion active Apple devices connect people, enable work and creativity, and features like Crash Detection, Fall Detection and ECG on Apple Watch have saved lives.

p2.evidence: Designing leading-edge chips and shipping roughly 250 million flawlessly made iPhones a year is extremely hard, though consumer devices are less critical to the world than, say, medicine or energy.

f1.evidence: Revenue grew from $274.5B (FY2020) to $416.2B (FY2025) in every year except FY2023 (-2.8%), and FY2026 nine-month sales are up strongly.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 38.2% (FY2020) to 46.9% (FY2025) and operating margin from 24.1% to 32.0%, helped by the growing Services mix.

f3.evidence: At June 2026 debt of $84.3B was below $146.5B of cash and marketable securities and is small against $117B of nine-month operating cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income doubled from $66.3B (FY2020) to $133.1B (FY2025), but operating cash flow peaked at $122.2B in FY2022 and was $111.5B in FY2025.

v1.evidence: Many see the iPhone as the best all-round phone because it is simple, secure, long-supported and works with other Apple gear, but Samsung and Google Pixel match or beat it on cameras and AI features.

v2.evidence: Apple ranks #1 on Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies list (for 18 straight years through 2025) and is a top target employer for engineering graduates.

c5.evidence: If Apple vanished, over a billion iPhone users, millions of app developers who earn from the App Store, and schools and hospitals using iPads would notice immediately.
